name: Thiruttani Murugan Temple
tradition: Kaumaram, the worship of Murugan within the Shaiva tradition
period: Early medieval hill shrine, expanded in later centuries
summary: Fifth of Murugan’s six abodes, Thiruttani on its low hill in the far north of Tamil Nadu is the place where, tradition says, the warrior god’s anger cooled after battle — a shrine of peace reached by 365 steps.

sections.history: Set on a hill in the north of the Tamil country near the Andhra border, Thiruttani has been a Murugan shrine since early times, developed across the Pallava and Chola periods and cherished by the Tamil hymnists. The saint-poet Arunagirinathar sang its praises in the Thiruppugazh, and in later centuries the composer Muthuswami Dikshitar was associated with the temple, so that Thiruttani holds a place in Tamil devotion and in the Carnatic musical tradition alike.
sections.architecture: The temple crowns a small hill reached by 365 steps, one for each day of the year, a climb that is itself a daily offering for many. The hilltop sanctum enshrines Subramanya with his consorts, and pillared halls and shrines cluster within the walls. The setting is open and airy, the plains of the northern Tamil country spreading below, and the modest scale of the complex lends it an intimacy that its great festival crowds only heighten.
sections.legends: Thiruttani takes its name and its character from peace. After the fierce war against the asuras, the god is said to have come here and let his anger subside — thani, to cool or settle — so that this is the abode of the pacified warrior. It is also honoured as a place linked to his union with Valli, the hunter’s daughter, whom he wooed away from the hills; and here the boy-god of victory is worshipped in his gentler aspect, granting calm to those who climb to him.
sections.festivals: The temple is famous for its New Year observance, when at the turn of the year vast crowds climb the 365 steps through the night to greet the first dawn before the god. Skanda Sashti, Vaikasi Visakam, and Thai Poosam are kept with processions and abhishekam, and the recitation of Arunagirinathar’s Thiruppugazh is especially dear here. Devotees carry milk and kavadi up the steps in fulfilment of vows through the festival season.
sections.experience: The climb of 365 steps sets the rhythm of a Thiruttani visit — an ascent counted in days, taken slowly, with the plains opening wider at each turn. At the top the air moves freely and the sanctum is calm, in keeping with the god’s peace that the place remembers. Many come at the New Year to begin the year at the god’s feet; others come on quiet mornings when only the wind and the bells are heard. The descent, with the whole country spread below, leaves visitors unhurried and settled.

visit.timings: Generally open from around 5:30 am to 9:00 pm daily, with abhishekams through the day; hours extend greatly at the New Year and during festivals.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — dhotis or trousers for men, sarees or salwar kameez for women, shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the foot of the hill.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted around the sanctum; follow posted rules and staff guidance, especially during festivals.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruttani is in Tiruvallur district, about 85 km from Chennai and close to the Andhra border; it has its own railway station on the Chennai–Renigunta line, and Chennai airport is the nearest.
